A statically typed language for coding agents and human authors · MIT OR Apache-2.0

Written by models,
read in your language.

Faber Romanus has a clear mechanical grammar, explicit static and generic types, and math-oriented operators. The same program renders in eight reader pack surfaces, and compiles to Rust, TypeScript, Go, Swift and more — so a library you write once can go into the project you already have.

No model? Install and run it yourself with one command.

Hand it to your model

Your model reads that file, downloads the current release for your machine, verifies its checksum, installs the faber command, and runs faber check on a hello program. It all happens on your machine.

The compiler front end, runner, standard library, and grammar are open source under MIT OR Apache-2.0. The official release also carries code generators that are not in the public source. Faber is experimental through version 1.

← main.fab · reader locale
faber convert --to en — English reader surface — the base spelling for everyday source
class Span {
    let f64 low
    let f64 high

    fn contains(f64 x) → bool {
        return self.low ≤ x and x ≤ self.high
    }

    fn center() → f64 {
        return (self.low + self.high) ÷ 2.0
    }
}

fn choose<T>(bool first, T a, T b) → T {
    return first ✓ a ✗ b
}

main {
    let Span bytes ← Span { low = 0.0, high = 255.0 }
    print bytes.center()
    print choose(bytes.contains(300.0), "inside", "outside")
    print -7 / 2
}

One program, eight readings. Every tab is the compiler’s own rendering (faber convert), and each one runs. Keywords, types and diagnostics change; identifiers and string literals do not.

Reader locales

Start in your own language

People should not need English to use a model for code, or to read what the model wrote. English is the maintained documentation tree; each reader locale has a mapping page, and source is written the same way: one reader locale per file, sealed against the others, so a Thai file contains Thai keywords and nothing else.

Englishen Latinla ภาษาไทยth-TH 简体中文zh-Hans 繁體中文zh-Hant Tiếng Việtvi العربيةar हिन्दीhi

Latin is the pack the language is named for. Reader locales also localize compiler diagnostics. See all languages · How reader locales work

Why Faber

Built for models to write

A model writes best against a surface with few surprises. Faber keeps the rules small, regular and explicit, then shows the result in the reader’s language.

  1. A mechanical grammar

    294 grammar productions, generated and checked as the parser’s authority. One construct has one spelling. Arrows mean runtime effects (← assign, → return, ⇥ error channel); = and : only state compile-time facts. Read the grammar

  2. Explicit static and generic types

    Declarations are type-first: f64 low, never low: f64. Nullability is written T ∪ none. Generics are written out (fn choose<T>), and crossing between integer and float is an explicit ↦, not an accident. Types and values

  3. Math-oriented operators

    Integer / floors, so -7 / 2 is -4; true division is ÷. Comparisons read as math (≤ ≥ ≢ ≈), and tensor work has its own operators (· matmul, ⊙ elementwise). When math and hardware convention disagree, Faber follows the math. Glyphs and Latin

  4. Machine-readable by design

    Diagnostics are coded and explainable. The documentation ships an agent index and focused skill guides at fixed paths, so a model can learn the language from the site itself. /llms.txt

Cross-compile

Write it once. Put it in the project you already have.

Faber compiles through one analyzed program to many targets. Write a library in Faber, emit it in the language your project already uses, and add it alongside your existing code. This small library, with no generics and no main, is emitted below exactly as faber emit produces it, and each panel was checked in its own toolchain.

// … 9 lines of generated header and runtime shim elided …

#[derive(Clone, PartialEq)]
pub struct Span {
    pub low: f64,
    pub high: f64,
}

impl ::core::fmt::Debug for Span {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut ::core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> ::core::fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "Span {{ low = {}, high = {} }}", faber::display::fractus(*&self.low), faber::display::fractus(*&self.high))
    }
}

impl Span {
    pub fn contains(&self, p_x: f64) -> bool {
        self.low <= p_x && p_x <= self.high
    }
    pub fn center(&self) -> f64 {
        (self.low + self.high) / 2.0
    }
}

class Span {
    low!: number;
    high!: number;
    toString(): string {
        return "Span { low = " + display.value(this.low, "fractus", { true_: "true", false_: "false", none: "none" }) + ", high = " + display.value(this.high, "fractus", { true_: "true", false_: "false", none: "none" }) + " }";
    }
    contains(p_x: number): boolean {
        return (this.low <= p_x) && (p_x <= this.high);
    }
    center(): number {
        return ((this.low + this.high) / 2);
    }
}

package main

type Span struct {
    Low float64
    High float64
}

func (self *Span) Contains(p_x float64) bool {
    return ((float64(self.Low) <= float64(p_x)) && (float64(p_x) <= float64(self.High)))
}

func (self *Span) Center() float64 {
    return float64(((self.Low + self.High) / 2.0))

faber emit --target swift span.fab — a source file; no runtime dependency
// Generated by radix - do not edit

func faberFractusPlain(_ description: String) -> String {
    var text = Substring(description)
    var sign = ""
    if text.hasPrefix("-") {
        sign = "-"
        text = text.dropFirst()
    }
    var exponent = 0
    if let marker = text.firstIndex(where: { $0 == "e" || $0 == "E" }) {
        exponent = Int(text[text.index(after: marker)...]) ?? 0
        text = text[..<marker]
    }
    var whole = Substring(text)
    var fraction = Substring("")
    if let dot = text.firstIndex(of: ".") {
        whole = text[..<dot]
        fraction = text[text.index(after: dot)...]
    }
    let digits = Array(String(whole) + String(fraction))
    let point = whole.count + exponent
    var shown: String
    if point <= 0 {
        shown = "0." + String(repeating: "0", count: -point) + String(digits)
    } else if point >= digits.count {
        shown = String(digits) + String(repeating: "0", count: point - digits.count) + ".0"
    } else {
        shown = String(digits[..<point]) + "." + String(digits[point...])
    }
    return sign + shown
}

func faberFractus64(_ value: Double) -> String {
    if value.isNaN { return "NaN" }
    if value.isInfinite { return value < 0 ? "-inf" : "inf" }
    if value.rounded(.towardZero) == value {
        let sign = value.sign == .minus ? "-" : ""
        let magnitude = value.magnitude
        if magnitude < 9.0e18 { return sign + String(UInt64(magnitude)) + ".0" }
        var digits = Array(String(magnitude.significandBitPattern | (UInt64(1) << 52)).utf8.reversed().map { $0 - 48 })
        for _ in 0..<(Int(magnitude.exponent) - 52) {
            var carry: UInt8 = 0
            for index in 0..<digits.count {
                let doubled = digits[index] * 2 + carry
                digits[index] = doubled % 10
                carry = doubled / 10
            }
            if carry > 0 { digits.append(carry) }
        }
        return sign + String(decoding: digits.reversed().map { $0 + 48 }, as: UTF8.self) + ".0"
    }
    return faberFractusPlain(value.description)
}

func faberFractus32(_ value: Float) -> String {
    if value.isNaN { return "NaN" }
    if value.isInfinite { return value < 0 ? "-inf" : "inf" }
    return faberFractusPlain(value.description)
}

class Span {
    var low: Double
    var high: Double

    init(low p_low: Double, high p_high: Double) {
        self.low = p_low
        self.high = p_high
    }

    func contains(x p_x: Double) -> Bool {
        return ((self.low <= p_x) && (p_x <= self.high))
    }

    func center() -> Double {
        return ((self.low + self.high) / 2.0)
    }
}

extension Span: CustomStringConvertible {
    var description: String { return "Span { low = \(faberFractus64(self.low)), high = \(faberFractus64(self.high)) }" }
}

Rust builds as a Cargo package today. TypeScript, Go and Swift give you source files to add to your project; assembling them into installable packages is not built yet. Support is stated target by target: generics and some operators do not lower to every target, and the target matrix records where. Read the target matrix

Libraries

Libraries written in Faber

The libraries are ordinary Faber source. They show what the language is for, and each one can be read, changed and emitted like your own code. Status is stated plainly.

Norma the standard library The default public library: text, JSON, TOML and YAML, files, HTTP, time, crypto, collections and math, imported as norma:*. Gradus autograd and ML Automatic differentiation, losses, optimizers and neural-network primitives. Models are pure functions; the backward pass is compiler-generated code. Triga graphics and geometry Scene graph, materials and geometry modeled on three.js shapes, written as a small, readable Faber library. Tela early; UI and view protocol Typed HTML and SVG view values with fail-closed validation and deterministic HTML and CSS output. The static renderer comes first. Inferentia in development A local-first GGUF inference server written in Faber. Today it is a command-line shell; model loading and HTTP serving are the next stages. Cista package store The package manager: install, resolve, inspect and cache Faber packages, independent of the compiler.

Example scenes built with Triga.

Grammar

A grammar you can read in one sitting

The language is specified as 294 productions in a single EBNF, generated from one source and published in full. It is large enough to be expressive and regular enough to hold in your head or a model’s context. The reference pages are generated from the same source, so they cannot disagree with the parser.

EBNF grammar Syntax guide Corpus of keyword examples Cheat sheet

Compute

Compute is one thing you can build

The same language carries numeric and device work. Tensor operators and kernel declarations lower to WGSL, Metal and CUDA routes, and Gradus uses them for autograd. Device execution is explicit and fail-closed: a requested backend never silently falls back to CPU. It is under active development; device inference is not shipped.
